## Source review flags

Places where the textbook (or its OCR) looked wrong, oversimplified or dated, and how the game's content handles each. Every flag is resolved in the content; sources are listed in each lesson file.

| Flag | Pages | Issue | Resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| L01-RF1 | p. 9, 10, 16 | Pages 9, 10 and 16 state that exactly 92 kinds of atoms occur naturally. The count depends on convention: Glenn Seaborg argued for 94 because trace plutonium forms in uranium ore, while some counts are lower because technetium and promethium occur only as tiny traces formed by uranium fission. | Content says “fewer than a hundred kinds of atoms occur in nature” and no question tests an exact natural-element count (as the brief requires). The textbook's 92 is treated as the figure used when the book was written. |
| L01-RF2 | p. 9, 10, 16 | The vocabulary box (p. 9) and p. 10 define an element as a unique particle of matter, which blurs the difference between an element and an atom. The Key Science Concept text (p. 16) gives the clearer definition: a substance made entirely of one kind of atom. | Glossary, cards and questions define an element as a substance made of only one kind of atom and an atom as a single particle of an element. |
| L01-RF3 | p. 9, 14 | Pages 9 and 14 say “all atoms of an element have the same atomic mass.” Most elements are natural mixtures of isotopes, so the value on the table is a weighted average and individual atoms differ slightly. | The glossary calls the printed value an average; no question claims every atom of an element has an identical mass; the O3 Explorer card names isotopes in its watch-out. Daltons are kept as the unit. |
| L01-RF4 | p. 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 | Pages 15, 18 and 19 describe the periodic table as organized by increasing atomic mass. L01-Q20 says mass “generally” increased along his rows. The O4 card watch-out and the Q27 explanation mention atomic number with external support. |

A generous box the size of the canyon (447 km long × 28.8 km maximum width × 1.6 km average depth ≈ 2.1 × 10¹³ m³) would be filled only about 80 times; using the 16 km average width, about 150 times. The real V-shaped canyon would be filled a few hundred times, not 500,000. | The Grand Canyon comparison is not used in any question or card. 'Billions of trillions' (10²¹ up to just under 10²⁴) fits anything from a small drop to about two teaspoons of water; OpenStax's 0.03 g drop holds about 10²¹ molecules. The same page's next sentence, about trillions of trillions of molecules, has the right scale. | Game text says 'trillions of trillions' or 'trillions upon trillions' of molecules: key idea 1, the O1 card, and, since round-1 review, Q02's explanation and evidence. # Per-lesson review records

## L01 — Atoms and Elements (printed pp. 8–19, PDF pp. 44–55)

Attraction: Neon Atom Midway. Files: `src/content/lessons/L01.json`, `src/content/questions/L01.json`.

### Source reading
- Text pages read: the whole OCR file `../tmp/lessons/L01.txt`, printed pp. 8–19 (PDF 44–55), including the vocabulary box, the NGSS box and the Lesson Summary.
- Rendered pages viewed (chapter PDF, 110 dpi): every page, 8–19. Extra checks:
  - p. 11 text at 220 dpi to read the exponents (5 × 10¹⁹ atoms per sand grain, 5 × 10⁵ Grand Canyon fills, 10⁻¹² m per picometer). OCR had mangled all three.
  - p. 15 (Mendeleev's 1871 table) at 260 dpi: the blanks are marked —=44 and —=68 (Gruppe III) and —=72 (Gruppe IV), plus —=100.
  - pp. 16–17 (Key Science Concept spread): the top of p. 17 and the lanthanide row at 200 dpi, to read the tile key (name, use icon, symbol, atomic mass) and the tile colours.
- Page offset checked: printed n + 36 = PDF n on every cited page (opener PDF p. 44 = printed p. 8; Lesson Summary PDF p. 55 = printed p. 19). Chapter-PDF page = printed − 7.

  | Section | Printed pp. |
  |---|---|

- Values used from the spread: H 1.008, He 4.0, Li 6.9, Na 23.0, K 39.1, Rb 85.5, Ca 40.1, Sr 87.6, Ba 137.3, Sc 45.0, O 16.0, Ne 20.2, Ar 39.9, Ga 69.7, Ge 72.6, Te 127.6, I 126.9, plus the copper (Cu) tile. From Mendeleev's 1871 table (p. 15): Te=125 just before J=127 (iodine).
- Round-1 revision (2026-10-14): re-rendered pp. 14, 16, 17 and 18 at 110 dpi and re-read the p. 15 zoom to confirm every value the revised questions use (He, Rb, Te, I, Se above Te, Cl and Br above I, Te=125/J=127).
- Brief seed question: included as L01-Q01 (why an air-filled balloon has more mass than the same empty balloon). It asks about mass, not a scale reading, and a `limitations` note covers buoyancy.

### Objectives
- L01-O1 (observe): identify matter, including invisible air, as anything with mass that takes up space; tell it apart from non-matter (light, sound); distinguish an atom from an element.
  - Families F01 (matter vs non-matter, seed), F02 (atom vs element), F03 (elements build substances; air is a mixture).
  - Questions Q01–Q07.
- L01-O2 (relate): the atomic scale and the tools it required, including the STM's criteria, constraints and probe-and-current model.
  - Families F04 (atomic scale), F05 (criteria vs constraints), F06 (STM current model), F09 (Q21, STM in the match).
  - Questions Q08–Q14 and Q21.
- L01-O3 (relate): patterns linking properties and atomic mass, from Döbereiner's trios to Mendeleev's predictive table.
  - Families F07 (trios and the column trend), F08 (Mendeleev's gaps and predictions), F09 (history and sequence), F12 (Q27, properties over mass order).
  - Questions Q15–Q22 and Q27.
- L01-O4 (apply): use position, atomic mass and chemical symbols to predict properties, identify an element, and interpret data.
  - Families F07 (Q16, predicting strontium's mass; Q17, extending the trend to rubidium), F10 (Q23, group predicts behaviour; Q24, identify an element from supplied properties), F11 (chemical symbols), F12 (reading mass data and exceptions).
  - Questions Q16, Q17 and Q23–Q28.
- Brief missions (section 7, entry 1): matter vs non-matter (Q01, Q02, Q03); identify an element using supplied properties (Q24, added in round 1); organize a set by a visible pattern (Q16, Q17, Q23).
- Mix after round 1: 8 foundational, 9 relationship, 11 application (was 9/9/10). Difficulty 1/2/3 = 5/21/2 (was 6/18/4; Q03 and Q14 recalibrated to 2, Q17 rewritten at 2).
- Types: single 15, multi 3, order 3, classify 3, match 2, numeric 2.
- 12 families, each with 2–3 questions; every follow-up points to another family.

### Review flags and resolutions
- L01-RF1: pp. 9, 10 and 16 give exactly 92 naturally occurring elements, but the count depends on convention (Seaborg argued for 94 because of trace plutonium). → Content says "fewer than a hundred"; no exact count is tested (brief requirement). Round 1: the issue text now says technetium and promethium occur only as tiny fission traces (not "essentially absent"). (Scientific American; RSC Periodic Table pages for technetium and promethium)
- L01-RF2: the vocabulary box (p. 9) and p. 10 define an element as a "unique particle", which blurs it with an atom. → Element = substance of only one kind of atom (the p. 16 wording); atom = one particle of an element. (OpenStax Chemistry 2e §1.2)
- L01-RF3: pp. 9 and 14 say all atoms of an element have the same atomic mass, which ignores isotopes. → The glossary calls the table value an average; no question asserts identical masses; the O3 card names isotopes. Match distractor r5 in Q21 targets the claim. (OpenStax §2.3)
- L01-RF4: pp. 15, 18 and 19 describe the table as ordered by atomic mass. The modern table is ordered by atomic number, and the spread itself puts Ar 39.9 before K 39.1 and Te 127.6 before I 126.9. → Questions keep "mostly increasing, with a few exceptions". The O4 card explains Ar/K through properties; round 1 moved Q27 to Te/I so the card no longer gives Q27's answer, and Q20 now says mass "generally" increased. Verifier correction: Mendeleev's 1871 table (p. 15) lists Te=125 before J=127, which is mass order by his own values, so the page does not show the pair "placed by properties"; the flag's resolution now says this. (OpenStax §2.5; NIH PubChem)
- L01-RF5: pp. 13 and 19 say the STM let people see atoms "for the first time" and "proved" atoms exist. → No question claims either. The STM is presented as a 1981 tool that maps surfaces atom by atom; the O2 card names the 1955 field ion microscope. Round 1: the O2 card's constraint sentence and Q11 item i3 no longer say "no existing technology" could show atoms; they say the available tools could not map the atoms of an ordinary surface. (Penn State Eberly College of Science; NobelPrize.org 1986 press release)
- L01-RF6: the p. 12 caption says "Greg Binnig". → Gerd Binnig is used throughout. (NobelPrize.org)
- L01-RF7: the p. 11 Grand Canyon comparison (500,000 fills) is off by roughly a thousandfold. A 40 mm ball is about 3.4 × 10⁻⁵ m³, so 5 × 10¹⁹ balls take up about 1.7 × 10¹⁵ m³. Even a generous canyon-sized box (447 × 28.8 × 1.6 km ≈ 2.1 × 10¹³ m³) would be filled only about 80 times, or about 150 times at the 16 km average width. → The comparison is not used anywhere. The sand-grain count is kept only as a rough, size-dependent estimate (Q10). (NPS Grand Canyon park statistics; Table Tennis England Laws, 40 mm ball)
- L01-RF8: p. 19 allows three-letter symbols, and the p. 18 figure shows Uut/Uup/Uus/Uuo. These are dated: IUPAC approved Nh, Mc, Ts and Og on 28 Nov 2016. → Content says one or two letters; nothing tests three-letter symbols. (IUPAC)
- L01-RF9: the Figure 5 caption (p. 18) says Li, Na and K all "burn" on contact with water, while p. 14 says lithium only fizzes. → Questions use the p. 14 account, reactivity Li < Na < K, with sodium that "can" start a fire (Q15, Q17, Q24); no procedures. Round 1: Q17 extends the trend to rubidium, which the textbook does not describe, so it carries outside evidence. (RSC Education; RSC Periodic Table, rubidium; OpenStax Chemistry 2e §18.1)
- L01-RF10: the spread's tile colours have no legend and are inconsistent (Tb blue and Lu pink, though both are solids). → Colours are never used. (NIH PubChem)
- L01-RF11: pp. 10 and 16 say "everything in the world" is made of atoms, and the brief asks for a matter vs non-matter mission. → Content says all *matter* is made of atoms; Q02 classifies light and sound as non-matter. (OpenStax §1.2; NASA Science, Anatomy of an Electromagnetic Wave)
- L01-RF12: OCR is garbled or empty on pp. 8, 11 (exponents), 15, 16–17 and 18. → All pages rendered; values read from renders (listed above and in the flag).

External sources were opened on 2026-10-14. The URLs are in `L01.json` → `reviewFlags[].evidence` and in each question's `evidence`.

### Review flags and resolutions
- L02-RF1: p. 22 says exactly 92 elements occur in nature, but the count depends on convention. → Content says "fewer than a hundred kinds of atoms", and no question tests the count (brief requirement); Q29 also says "fewer than a hundred". (Scientific American, Seaborg's 94)
- L02-RF2: OCR is empty or garbled on pp. 20, 24, 25, 27 and 28, including every subscript. → All pages rendered; every value used was read from the renders, and the vitamin C model was counted from the p. 20 render. (PubChem formulas)
- L02-RF3: the Figure 3A caption (p. 26) says quartz is 1 O : 1 Si, which contradicts the main text's correct 1 Si : 2 O. → Content uses 1:2 (SiO₂). Q18 carries the 1:1 version as unmatched distractor r6 and now explains the slip in its feedback; Q19 computes silicon from oxygen at 1:2. The O3 card names the caption error. (RSC, silicon; PubChem, silica O2Si)
- L02-RF4: p. 24 (and the Figure 2A photo) presents hydrogen peroxide on cuts as normal first aid, which is dated advice. → No first-aid or home-use content; hydrogen peroxide appears only as a different substance used as a disinfectant, never drunk. (Houston Methodist; MedlinePlus)
- L02-RF5: p. 25 calls isobutane "triangle-like" (text) and "pyramid-like" (figure label). → Content says "branched: one central carbon joined to the other three". (PubChem isobutane: propane with a methyl group at position 2)
- L02-RF6: p. 23's "line-angle formulas" description (every atom drawn with its symbol) actually describes structural formulas; skeletal drawings omit C and H. → The term is not used or tested. (OpenStax Organic Chemistry §1.12; OpenStax Chemistry 2e §2.4)
- L02-RF7: p. 23 says everyone uses the same colors for each element. This is a common convention (CPK), and carbon is often gray rather than black. → Colors are called a convention, diagrams label atoms by symbol, and Q05 tests that colors are labels. (Imperial College, Atom Colours)
- L02-RF8: pp. 27–29 simplify polymers. They call the subunit "always a molecule" and say polyester repeats "ester molecules", yet a polymer chain is usually counted as one macromolecule. Proteins and DNA mix different units in a set order, so they have no single ratio. → The lesson's model is kept. Only synthetic polymers illustrate repeating units. Round 1 removed "a protein" from the polymer glossary entry, because it contradicted this flag. Proteins and DNA appear only as natural-polymer examples (Q23, the O3 card, the Q24 hint). Q17's prompt now names its five structures, so proteins and DNA are outside it. The O3 card's watch-out names the issue. (LibreTexts polymer definition; OpenStax Organic Chemistry §31.4; OpenStax Biology 2e §3.4 and §3.5)
- L02-RF9: pp. 26 and 28 call salt's particles atoms, but they are ions. → "Atoms" is kept, since MS-PS1-1's assessment boundary excludes the ionic nature of subunits. The O3 card mentions ions. NaCl is consistently treated as a ratio, not a molecule (Q15, Q16, Q18). Q16 and Q18 speak of solid salt, because NaCl ion pairs exist in hot vapor. (OpenStax Chemistry 2e §2.6; NGSS MS-PS1-1)
- L02-RF10: p. 28 says cholesterol is arranged in "six-sided rings". Its steroid core has three six-membered rings and one five-membered ring. → Only the atom counts (C₂₇H₄₆O, 74 atoms) are used. (OpenStax Organic Chemistry §27.6; PubChem)
- L02-RF11: p. 29 makes absolute claims: snowflakes "always have six sides" and every salt grain is the same cube. → Content says "tend to", and objective O4 now says "six-fold symmetry" and "cube-like". Q27 and Q28 carry limitations, and the O4 card names the overstatement. (NOAA NESDIS; Libbrecht, Caltech SnowCrystals.com field guide; LibreTexts Mineralogy, halite)
- L02-RF12: p. 29 says diamond is "bonded in a cubic shape", and p. 26 calls its subunit a "cage". → Content says each carbon is locked to neighbors in every direction in a rigid 3D network. (OpenStax Chemistry 2e §10.5)
- L02-RF13: p. 22 lists hydrogen among the elements in the air we breathe; H₂ is only about 0.55 ppm of dry air. → Not used anywhere. (NASA Earth Fact Sheet)
- L02-RF14 (new, round 1): p. 29 says diamonds are good cutting tools for steel. Diamond is hard enough, but at cutting temperatures its carbon reacts with the iron (for example, turning to graphite with iron as a catalyst), so it wears quickly on steel; cubic boron nitride is widely used for machining and grinding ferrous metals. → Key idea 8, the O4 card and the O4 table no longer say diamond cuts steel. Q26 asks for a "very hard" edge, says diamond-tipped blades can cut very hard materials including steel, and has a limitation naming chemical wear and cubic boron nitride. (NIST: Lane, Dow and Scattergood, Wear 2013, abstract; Google Patents US 4,563,114; Fujisaki et al. 2009, Hokkaido University HUSCAP)
- L02-RF15 (new, round 1): p. 23 says stronger bonds are drawn with several sticks and weaker bonds with dotted sticks. Several sticks mark double or triple bonds, which are stronger only than a single bond between the same two atoms. Dotted lines usually mark much weaker attractions such as hydrogen bonds, often drawn between molecules. → Not used in content: every model uses single sticks only. (OpenStax Chemistry 2e §7.3, §7.5, §10.1)
- L02-RF16 (new, round 1): p. 21 calls a vitamin C molecule "millions of times smaller" than a printed period and "one of the smaller molecules". The comparison depends on whether width or volume is meant and on the print size, and a 20-atom molecule is small but not among the smallest (O₂ has 2 atoms, water 3). → Not used in content. No external source giving a period's width was found, so the flag states no figure of its own; its evidence is the textbook's own pages (21, 22, 28).

External sources were opened on 2026-10-14. The URLs are in `L02.json` → `reviewFlags[].evidence` and in each question's `evidence`. Pages I tried that returned errors or no usable text, and so are not cited:

### Review flags and resolutions
- **L03-RF1** (pp. 34, 38): the Key Science Concept says the 2.7 g/cm³ sample is "too dense to be made of silver". Silver is about 10.5 g/cm³, so the sample is far less dense than silver. The arithmetic and the aluminum conclusion are right.
  - Resolution: Q26 asks which results rule out silver, and the O5 card's watch-out names the error. No game text repeats "too dense". (Round 1: Q26's misconception field no longer mentions the textbook slip, because it is a book error, not a learner belief. Round 2: O5 paragraph 2 rules out palladium instead of silver, so the card no longer gives away Q26's data.)
  - Sources: textbook pp. 34, 38; PubChem.
- **L03-RF2** (pp. 36, 38): metals "dissolving" in acids (silver in nitric acid, platinum in aqua regia, aluminum in three acids) are chemical reactions that make new substances, unlike sugar dissolving in water.
  - Resolution: solubility items use only sugar/flour and marker inks; no acid test appears in any question; the O4 card's watch-out explains the difference, and since round 1 its diagram says solubility keeps the substance the same only "for true dissolving (sugar in water)". I could not open a source on aluminum in nitric acid, so that detail is neither used nor corrected. The science reviewer noted that concentrated nitric acid passivates aluminum; the change was optional and no source was opened in round 1, so RF2 is unchanged.
  - Sources: OpenStax 4.2 (metal + acid redox, Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂) and 1.3 (sugar dissolving is a physical change).
- **L03-RF3** (pp. 33, 35, 39): identifying properties are said to "never change". Boiling point depends on air pressure: water boils at about 90 °C in Leadville, Colorado. Odor is a weak identifier, and many substances have none.
  - Resolution: prompts say "pure" and "same conditions" or "ordinary air pressure"; Q18 repairs the idea; the rewritten Q16 compares boiling points at the same pressure; the glossary's boiling-point entry names sea-level pressure; no question uses odor as an identifier.
  - Source: OpenStax 10.3 (normal boiling point at 1 atm; Leadville example).
- **L03-RF4** (pp. 31, 33): steel beams, glass and "copper" pennies are presented as single substances. Steel is an alloy; glass has several ingredients; pennies are copper alloys or copper-plated zinc. The rendered p. 33 photos show green corrosion on both the statue and the coins.
  - Round 1: the penny detail is also dated. A science reviewer's web search reported the U.S. Mint struck its final circulating penny on 2025-11-12. The Mint's press release returned HTTP 403, so it is not cited, and no game text relies on the date. The O1 watch-out now says "modern U.S. pennies are mostly zinc with a thin copper coating" instead of "today's pennies", and the U.S. Mint record's supports line no longer says "Today's penny".
  - Round 2: the second science reviewer's web search (dated 2026-10-17) found consistent reports, for example CoinNews and NBC, of a ceremonial final strike at the Philadelphia Mint on 12 November 2025, with pennies remaining legal tender. The reviewer marked this informational, needing no change. RF4's issue text records it, and the date stays uncited because none of those outlets is on the guide's preferred list.
  - Resolution: the O1 card's watch-out names these as mixtures; Q05 uses imagined pure-copper objects and says so in its `limitations`.
  - Sources: OpenStax 3.3 (steel is an alloy) and 1.2 (glass with added elements; pure-substance definition); U.S. Mint Coin Classroom (penny is copper over a zinc core); American Ceramic Society (the statue's green surface comes from copper oxidizing in air and sea spray).
- **L03-RF5** (p. 37): the text says flammable gases "will always ignite" and that a non-flammable gas may put a splint out. Ignition depends on the mix with air, and oxygen relights a glowing splint.
  - Resolution: Q22 describes hydrogen already mixed with air and asks only which property is tested; no gas procedure is given.
  - Sources: RSC "Combustion of hydrogen in air" (best pop at 20–40% hydrogen) and "The preparation and properties of oxygen".
- **L03-RF6** (p. 37): octane is called "the main component of gasoline"; gasoline is a blend.
  - Resolution: neither gasoline nor octane appears in any question or card.
  - Sources: EIA "Gasoline explained"; OpenStax 1.2 (gasoline is a homogeneous mixture).
- **L03-RF7** (pp. 34, 35, 38): number check.
  - Every textbook value matches PubChem within rounding: Ag 10.5 g/cm³ and about 960 °C; Pt 21.5; Pd 12.0 and about 1550 °C; Al 2.7 and 660 °C.
  - Magnesium (1.74 g/cm³, 650 °C), gold (19.3 g/cm³, 1064 °C) and platinum's melting point (about 1768 °C) are not in the textbook. They come from PubChem, whose melting points are given in kelvin and were converted, and they are cited wherever they are used (Q07, Q17, Q24, Q25, O5 card). Round 2 added platinum's melting point and Q07 to RF7; the O5 table had already used 1768 °C.
- **L03-RF8** (pp. 31, 37): physical versus chemical property is never defined. Only the p. 37 caption calls flammability a chemical property.
  - Resolution: Q23 carries the distinction with external support. The glossary defines "chemical property" and, since round 1, "physical property" (named only in the p. 31 standards box; definition rests on OpenStax 1.3). Round 2: Q29 uses flammability to tell two lookalike wires apart. Its white-powder product rests on RSC and the PubChem magnesium oxide record.
  - Sources: OpenStax 1.3; RSC magnesium page (2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO).
- **L03-RF9** (p. 32, new in round 1): the book says a cup of water holds "billions of trillions of atoms". A 250 mL cup is about 13.9 mol, about 8.4 × 10²⁴ molecules or 2.5 × 10²⁵ atoms: trillions of trillions, roughly 25 to 25,000 times more, depending on how many billions are meant. "Billions of trillions" (10²¹ up to just under 10²⁴ atoms) fits anything from a small drop to about two teaspoons of water; OpenStax's 0.03 g drop holds about 10²¹ molecules.
  - Round 2: the science reviewer found that "about ten thousand times too few" is true only at the low end of the range. The RF9 issue text and this bullet now give the 25-to-25,000 range. I also replaced "fits a single small drop", because the top of the range is about 10 g of water (10²⁴ atoms ÷ 3 = 3.3 × 10²³ molecules ≈ 0.55 mol ≈ 10 g). Q02's round-1 note was corrected to match. No learner text is affected.
  - Resolution: key idea 1 and the O1 card already said "trillions upon trillions"; Q02's explanation and evidence now say "trillions of trillions of water molecules". No game text repeats the understated figure.
  - Sources: textbook p. 32; OpenStax 3.1 (Avogadro's number, about 18 g per mole of water, the 0.03 g drop example).
- **L03-RF10** (p. 37, new in round 1): the book's magnesium wire bursts into flame when heated to find its melting point, yet the game uses magnesium's melting point (O5 card, O5 table, Q25).
  - Resolution: Q25 says the strip is heated in argon gas so it cannot burn (prompt and `conditions`), and O5 paragraph 3 says the comparison is "measured without air, because hot magnesium catches fire". No question asks a learner to melt or burn magnesium.
  - Sources: textbook p. 37; PubChem; RSC magnesium page (burning combines magnesium with oxygen); OpenStax 18.12 (argon's chemical inertness).

### Objectives
- L04-O1 (observe): identify producers on land and in water and the cell structures (chloroplasts) where most of them capture light; tell the energy input apart from the matter inputs. (Round 1: "leaf structures" became "cell structures", because algae and cyanobacteria have no leaves, and the objective was split into two sentences.)
  - Families: F01 (energy vs matter inputs), F02 (producers and where they can make food: Q03 asks what counts as a producer, Q05 asks why light limits where phytoplankton grow), F03 (chloroplasts, chlorophyll, light color).
  - Questions: Q01–Q03, Q05–Q08 (Q04 rejected).
- L04-O2 (relate): use the balanced equation to explain atoms being rearranged (none gained or lost) while light energy is stored as chemical energy.
  - Families: F01 (Q02), F04 (reading and reasoning with the equation), F05 (what happens to light energy: Q11 repairs the shorthand "turns sunlight into sugar", Q12 follows the absorbed energy), F07 (Q16).
  - Questions: Q02, Q09–Q12, Q16.
  - Round 2: Q11's misconception is now about misreading a shorthand statement, so F05 no longer shares F01's "sunlight becomes part of the sugar" target (Q02). A future F05 item should be about where light energy goes (for example, some becomes heat), not "sunlight is not matter".
- L04-O3 (apply): use experimental evidence to explain where plant matter comes from, and predict the effect of changing light or carbon dioxide.
  - Families: F02 (Q05), F03 (Q08), F06 (Ingenhousz: conclusion, fair test, respiration in light), F07 (evidence for where plant matter comes from: Q16 asks what the evidence shows, Q17 asks how to tell observations in a sealed-jar study from conclusions), F08 (predicting condition changes).
  - Round 2: the pedagogy review noted that F02 and F07 each join two related skills. Neither can be split without leaving a one-question family, so the shared ideas are written out here, and the family-based mastery rule counts them knowingly.
  - Questions: Q05, Q08, Q13–Q19.
- L04-O4 (relate): explain how producers use, store and build with sugar, and how biomass passes matter and energy to eaters.
  - Families: F06 (Q15), F08 (Q19), F09 (uses of sugar, cellulose), F10 (carbon path into a person, energy path to a lion, what counts as biomass).
  - Questions: Q15, Q19–Q23, Q29.

  - Families: F10 (Q29), F11 (criteria vs constraints, energy per kilogram), F12 (choosing a biomass source, biofuel CO₂, crop trade-off).

### Review flags and resolutions
- **L04-RF1** (pp. 42, 47, 48)
  - Issue: OCR is unusable on the opener and garbles the photosynthesis equation and the Key Science Concept labels. The p. 47 text also calls the equation a "chemical formula".
  - Resolution: read from the renders (Figure 2B also at 220 dpi). The equation is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, with 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side. Content says "chemical equation" for the whole reaction and "formula" for each substance.
  - Sources: textbook pp. 47–48 (rendered).
- **L04-RF2** (pp. 43, 46–48, 50, 53)
  - Issue: energy is described as "stored in chemical bonds", and cells "release the energy stored in the bonds". Taken literally, that contradicts the guardrail that breaking bonds requires energy.
  - Resolution: content says light energy ends up stored as chemical energy in sugar and is released when sugar reacts with oxygen. The O2 watchOut explains the shorthand, and no question asks where in a molecule energy sits. The rewritten Q12 keys "stored as chemical energy in the sugar" and "released when the sugar reacts with oxygen", never bond breaking.
  - Sources: RSC Education, "Chemical energetics: words matter". OpenStax Biology 2e 8.1 shows the shorthand is common. OpenStax Biology 2e 6.3 (energy changes form; some becomes heat) backs Q12.
- **L04-RF3** (p. 46)
  - Issue: the text says chlorophyll does not absorb green light. In fact, leaves absorb about 70–80 percent of green light (about 90 percent of red and blue), and absorbed green light drives photosynthesis.
  - Resolution: Q07 is keyed to "absorbs less green than red or blue". Q08 is now a one-hour test on two leaves and predicts that the green-lit leaf still makes some sugar; its explanation tells learners the textbook's wording is a simplification. The O1 watchOut covers it.
  - Source: The University of Tokyo, "Why are leaves green?" (Terashima).
- **L04-RF4** (pp. 49–50)
  - Issue: the Figure 3 labels can be read as "plants give off CO₂ only in the dark". Brief guardrail: plants photosynthesize and respire.
  - Resolution: Q15 teaches that sugar breakdown continues day and night and that photosynthesis outpaces it in bright light. Q18's limitation and Q20's "leaf cell at midnight" carry the same point. The O3 watchOut covers it.
  - Sources: Encyclopedia of the Environment (Dizengremel, Université de Lorraine); Botany online (University of Hamburg); textbook p. 50.
- **L04-RF5** (p. 49)
  - Issue: the textbook's "about 70 percent from carbon dioxide, most of the rest from water" for Saussure does not match modern dry-mass estimates. Those put about 90 percent (carbon plus oxygen) as tracing to CO₂, about 6 percent hydrogen from water, and about 4 percent soil minerals.
  - Resolution: the percentage is never tested. Q16 says "most" and defines dry mass; its rationales use the 4 and 6 percent figures.
  - Sources: Carbon TIME (Michigan State University, re-opened 2026-10-15); Botany online (University of Hamburg; also van Helmont's willow).
- **L04-RF6** (pp. 43, 51)
  - Issue: p. 51 says "all other organisms" depend on photosynthesis, while p. 43 says "nearly all". Chemosynthetic vent and seep communities are the exception.
  - Resolution: content says "nearly all", and the O4 watchOut now names vent and seep communities. Q23 uses a single grassland chain.
  - Source: NOAA Ocean Exploration, photosynthesis vs chemosynthesis (re-opened 2026-10-15; names hydrothermal vents and cold seeps).
- **L04-RF7** (p. 45)
  - Issue: the text says cyanobacteria live in "boiling-hot" springs. Their growth limit is about 70–74 °C.
  - Resolution: content does not repeat the hot-spring claim, and no question tests the temperature. (Round 1 corrected this resolution, which had described content that does not exist.)
  - Source: University of Edinburgh, The Microbial World (Deacon), Yellowstone thermophiles.
- **L04-RF8** (pp. 52–53)
  - Issue: the biofuel section is dated or simplified:
    - It calls jet biofuel "low-cost". As of 2026, IATA reports that it costs several times more than conventional jet fuel and expects it to be under 1 percent of jet fuel use (about 0.8 percent, about 2.4 Mt).
    - It says sugars become "alcohol that is used as fuel". In practice, alcohols are upgraded into jet-fuel hydrocarbons and blended with conventional fuel.
    - It uses "efficient" for energy per unit mass.
  - Resolution: questions test the criteria, constraints and trade-off reasoning, not market claims. Q26's limitation and the O5 card give the dated (as of 2026) figures, content uses "energy per kilogram", and Q27 repairs "biofuel releases no CO₂" (the textbook itself says it does).
  - Round 2: Q26's prompt now says "In the textbook's design story". Q26 key e and the O5 card keep the textbook's hedge ("might go to landfills"; "might otherwise go to a landfill"), because much city cardboard is recycled and many yard trimmings are composted.
  - Sources: IATA SAF page (re-opened 2026-10-15); U.S. DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center (SAF); U.S. DOE Alternative Fuels and Feedstocks Office (SAF).
- **L04-RF9** (p. 50)
  - Issue: cellulose "looks like many sugar molecules bound together". Each link leaves out the atoms of one water molecule (each unit is glucose minus H₂O).
  - Resolution: content says "linked sugar units". Round 2 changed the Q21 explanation, the O4 watchOut and this flag from "a water molecule is given off at each link" to "each link leaves out the atoms of one water molecule".
    - Reason (science review): water given off at each link is the classroom dehydration-synthesis model. The reviewer noted that plant cellulose synthase adds glucose from UDP-glucose and releases UDP.
    - Content makes no mechanism claim, so that point needs no source here. The composition wording is exact either way.
  - Source: OpenStax Biology 2e 3.2 Carbohydrates (glucose polymers; composition).
- **L04-RF10** (p. 50), new in round 1
  - Issue: the Figure 4 caption says cellulose "makes up the bulk of plant bodies". Read as "most of a plant", that overstates it: dry wood is about 38–49 percent cellulose.
  - Resolution: content calls cellulose the main material of plant cell walls and the largest single ingredient of wood, with cotton as the nearly pure example (glossary, Q21). Q20 says a cell wall is built mainly from cellulose. Evidence records quote the textbook's "the bulk of plant bodies" instead of "most". No question asks what share of a plant is cellulose.
  - Sources: USDA Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory, "Cell wall chemistry" (Rowell, Pettersen et al. 2005); Frontiers in Plant Science, Haigler et al. 2012 (mature cotton fiber > 90 percent cellulose); OpenStax Biology 2e 3.2.
- **L04-RF11** (p. 49), new in round 2
  - Issue: Figure 3 labels "oxygen bubbles" on potted plants kept in air under glass jars, and the text says Ingenhousz collected and analyzed bubbles of gas. Visible gas bubbles form only on plants under water; in the rendered figure the "bubbles" are drawn molecule callouts. Ingenhousz's own bubble observations used leaves plunged in jars of water.
  - Resolution:
    - The O3 card's Ingenhousz paragraph now describes leaves in jars of water gathering bubbles in sunshine and hardly any after sunset. A new paragraph separates his observations from his conclusion. The table row and alt text match, and the watchOut says the drawn bubbles are symbols.
    - Q13 and Q14 keep the textbook's potted-plant setup but speak of oxygen given off, not bubbles. Q17 now states a water plant sealed in a jar of water.
  - Sources: textbook p. 49 Figure 3 (rendered); Le Moyne College, Classic Chemistry website, Ingenhousz, *Experiments upon Vegetables* (1779), excerpt (opened 2026-10-17).
    - The excerpt calls the gas "dephlogisticated air" and never says "oxygen".
    - The card's "turned out to be rich in oxygen" therefore rests on the textbook's p. 49 statement that the green parts produce oxygen in light.
- Not flagged:
  - The p. 45 statements that phytoplankton (including diatoms and cyanobacteria) photosynthesize near the sunlit surface are consistent with NASA Earth Observatory "What are Phytoplankton?" (opened). No external record was needed, because Q05 rests on the textbook page.
  - Historical dates (Ingenhousz late 1700s, Saussure early 1800s) match Botany online. They are used only in the O3 card, not tested.

### Review flags and resolutions
- **L05-RF1** (pp. 59, 60, 63): the OCR garbles every formula and arrow, and the p. 59 Figure 3B art prints a stray "+" before the arrow.
  - Resolution: the equation was taken from the renders and hand-checked, and the stray plus is never reproduced. Since round 1, Q09 traces hydrogen into water, Q10 uses the 6 O₂-per-sugar ratio, and Q11 checks conservation of mass.
  - Sources: textbook p. 60 (KSC equation); OpenStax Biology 2e 3.2 and 8.1.
- **L05-RF2** (p. 59): the text says producers don't need to take in oxygen because photosynthesis already supplies it. That is wrong for roots, seeds and every plant cell at night.
  - Resolution: Q20 repairs it with flooded-root evidence. Q17 shows respiration continuing in the dark, using a plant in sterile sand so that soil microbes add no carbon dioxide. The O3 card names the issue.
  - Round 2: Q17 now asks how much carbon dioxide photosynthesis alone removed in the light (150 + 60 = 210 ppm each hour), which works only if respiration keeps running in the light. Because the Ohio State page covers only night, an Encyclopedia of the Environment article (Dizengremel, Université de Lorraine) was added for respiration by day and night.
  - The Ohio State page is cited only for what it says: non-green parts respire, and green parts respire at night. The "day and night" wording in the content is general knowledge, not attributed to that page.
  - Sources: University of Missouri Extension, "Too much moisture can hinder root development"; Ohio State University PlantFacts, "Respiration".
- **L05-RF3** (p. 58, Figure 3A): the text says "every cell" has mitochondria, "most unicellular organisms" have them, and respiration takes place in them.
  - Corrections: mature red blood cells lack mitochondria; bacteria and archaea have none; glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm.
  - Resolution: content says "most of" respiration happens in mitochondria, which plant cells, animal cells and many single-celled organisms have. Q14 is keyed to "most of the work". Since round 1, Q23 says respiration happens "mostly in the mitochondria", and Q24 names cellular respiration without placing all of it there.
  - Sources: OpenStax Biology 2e 7.2 and 4.2; OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e 18.3.
- **L05-RF4** (pp. 57, 59, 61, 63): the text says energy is "stored in bonds" and released "as the molecule is broken down", and that respiration "generates" energy. It also says producers can't use light energy directly.
  - Resolution: no game text says that breaking bonds releases energy or that energy is created. Q12 repairs "creates energy"; Q13 teaches the net picture (forming the stronger CO₂ and H₂O bonds releases more than breaking the old ones costs). The O2 card's watchOut names the shortcut.
  - Round 1: the p. 57 idea now appears only in its defensible form, light energy stored in sugar so it can travel to cells that aren't capturing light. This covers Q07's explanation, the O1 card's third paragraph and its watchOut, and Q16's choice b rationale.
  - Sources: OpenStax Chemistry 2e 7.5; OpenStax Biology 2e 6.3.
- **L05-RF5** (pp. 55–56): herbivores, including the acorn-eating squirrel, are called predators.
  - Resolution: content uses "consumer" throughout, and no question asks about predators.
  - Source: OpenStax Biology 2e 45.6, which treats herbivory as separate from predation.
- **L05-RF6** (p. 57, Figure 2): the table lists soil as a source of plant matter.
  - Resolution (round 1): Q03 item s6 (producers get the carbon for their bodies from carbon dioxide) carries the point. The O1 card table says "plus small amounts of soil minerals", and its watchOut explains it. Q04, the original plant-mass item, was rejected as a duplicate of L04-Q16, because L04 teaches plant mass.
  - Source: OpenStax Biology 2e 31.1 (carbon is most of a plant's dry mass).
- **L05-RF7** (p. 57): the text says consumers don't use the water they take in to build cells.
  - Resolution: Q05 asks only about carbon atoms. Since round 1, its drinking-water distractor and its limitation both say that water also becomes part of cells.
  - Source: USGS Water Science School, "The Water in You" (up to 60% of an adult body is water).
- **L05-RF8** (p. 61): the text says food is digested into small molecules in the stomach.
  - Resolution: no question names an organ. Q23 (now a baked potato) orders chewing, then digestion "finishing" the starch, then transport in the blood. The O4 card gives the corrected sequence: mouth, stomach, then the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed.
  - Source: NIDDK, "Your Digestive System & How It Works".
- **L05-RF9** (p. 62): the text says no animal can make cellulose, but tunicates do.
  - Resolution: content says "your body can't make cellulose". Since round 1, Q21 matches cellulose to "forms the tough walls of plant cells", so it no longer depends on the claim.
  - Sources: the OIST seminar page, supplemented in round 1 by the OIST Institutional Repository record of Inoue, Nakashima and Satoh (2019), *Genes* 10: 294. Its abstract says tunicates are the only metazoans that can synthesize cellulose.
  - The PMC copy of that paper (PMC6523144) returned a reCAPTCHA page and MDPI returned HTTP 403, so the repository record was cited instead.
- **L05-RF10** (p. 62): a fat is defined as storing energy "in the form of oils".
  - Resolution: the glossary says oils are fats that are liquid at room temperature, and no question tests it.
  - Round 2 addition: cell membranes are built mainly from phospholipids, close relatives of fats made partly from fatty acids. "Fats help build membranes" (glossary, Q21 r2, Q24 i5, following p. 62) is kept as a grade-level simplification, and no question says membranes are made of fat.
  - Source: OpenStax Biology 2e 3.3 (re-opened in round 2: phospholipids are major membrane constituents and, like fats, are built from fatty acid chains on a glycerol backbone).
- **L05-RF11** (p. 63): the mirror-image word equations can suggest one reaction running backward.
  - Resolution: the O5 card's watchOut explains that the equations summarize different multistep pathways in different places, and that the oxygen comes from water. Q25 compares the gases and who carries out each process; Q26 compares energy and carries a limitation saying the equations are summaries.
  - Sources: OpenStax Biology 2e 8.2 and 7.2.
- **L05-RF12** (pp. 56, 63; new in round 1): consumers are defined as organisms that can't make food by photosynthesis, and producers only by capturing sunlight. Chemosynthetic producers, such as deep-sea vent bacteria, make food without light and are not consumers.
  - Resolution: the glossary, key idea 1 and Q01 now define a consumer as an organism that can't make its own food. The glossary says most producers, not all, use sunlight. Q03's conditions limit it to typical producers and consumers.
  - Round 2: the science reviewer found that key idea 2 ("Producers build that sugar ... using light") and the photosynthesis glossary entry ("plants, algae and other producers") still said every producer uses light. Key idea 2 and the photosynthesis glossary entry were narrowed to photosynthetic producers in science review round 2: "Plants and other photosynthetic producers" and "plants, algae and some bacteria". Q02's read-aloud prompt no longer says producers make food "by photosynthesis".
  - Source: NOAA Ocean Exploration, "What is the difference between photosynthesis and chemosynthesis?"
- **L05-RF13** (p. 62; new in round 2): two oversimplifications. The page explains the name "simple carbohydrate" by the small number of atoms in a sugar; sugars are called simple because each is a single sugar unit, or two joined. It also defines a carbohydrate as an energy-storage molecule, though cellulose, named on the same page, is structural.
  - Resolution: the glossary defines a carbohydrate as storing energy or building structure, the O4 card calls complex carbohydrates long chains of sugars, and since round 2 the O4 card says "many" carbohydrates are energy molecules. No question uses either textbook wording, and Q21 matches cellulose to plant cell walls.
  - Source: OpenStax Biology 2e 3.2 (re-opened in round 2: monosaccharides are the simple sugars; polysaccharides are long chains of them; cellulose makes up most of a plant cell wall).
- Brief guardrail ("breathing is not identical to cellular respiration"): taught in the O3 card and tested in Q18 and Q19, with breathing distractors in Q13 and Q15. Q17's breathing distractor was removed when it was rewritten in round 2.
  - Round 2: breathing now has one definition everywhere: animals with lungs or gills move air or water over them so gases can be exchanged. This covers key idea 5, the O3 card's paragraph 3 and watchOut, Q18's key rationale and explanation, and Q19's i5 rationale.
  - Before, the lesson called breathing "gas exchange" while also saying a plant "never breathes", even though plant cells exchange gases.
- Energy and matter guardrail:
  - Q28 (closed terrarium) carries "energy is recycled too" as a distractor.
  - Key idea 7 says energy leaves as heat while matter cycles.
  - Q29's explanation says fat's atoms end up in carbon dioxide and water.
- Branching-cycle guardrail: Q27 now carries a limitation that its carbon route is one of many.

### Review flags and resolutions
- **L06-RF1** (pp. 65, 72; the brief's p. 72–73 check)
  - Issue: the Key Science Concept text says energy "cycles" through an ecosystem, and the Introduction says energy and matter are recycled.
  - Decision: energy flows one way and leaves as heat; only matter cycles. The spread's arrows themselves are correct (food to eater, and every organism to decomposers).
  - Resolution: Q11 sorts matter-only, energy-only and shared statements, and Q12 repairs the "energy cycles" wording.
  - Sources: OpenStax Biology 2e 46.2 and 46.3; textbook p. 71.
- **L06-RF2** (pp. 70, 72–73)
  - Issue: the text says matter is "lost" moving up a food web.
  - Resolution: content says matter leaves the food chain as wastes, as respired carbon dioxide and water, or in remains that go to decomposers. Q10 and Q14–Q16 carry "destroyed" and "turned into energy" as distractors.
  - Sources: OpenStax 46.3; textbook p. 70.
- **L06-RF3** (p. 71)
  - Issue: the textbook presents 10 percent as exact.
  - Resolution: questions state "use the 10 percent model" as a condition. Q20 computes 12 percent from example data, and the O3 card calls 10 percent an average.
  - Sources: National Geographic Education "Energy Flow and the 10 Percent Rule"; OpenStax 46.2 (the Silver Springs example is about 14.5 percent).
- **L06-RF4** (p. 72)
  - Issue: the text says "populations get smaller at each level." Pyramids of numbers, and some aquatic biomass pyramids, can be inverted; energy pyramids (energy passed up per area per year) cannot.
  - Resolution: Q18 uses an oak tree that feeds thousands of caterpillars. Round 1: content now says the energy *passed up* to a level always shrinks (not the energy a level "holds"). Q16 now compares new biomass built over a year, with a limitation naming the inverted open-ocean plankton snapshot.
  - Source: OpenStax 46.2 (English Channel inverted biomass pyramid; upright energy pyramids in kcal/m²/yr).
- **L06-RF5** (p. 70)
  - Issue: the text calls zooplankton "single-celled consumers." Many are small animals, and the book's own art shows crustaceans.
  - Resolution: the glossary describes zooplankton as tiny drifting consumers, many of them small animals. No question tests whether they are single-celled.
  - Source: NOAA National Ocean Service, "What are plankton?"
- **L06-RF6** (pp. 66, 67, 69)
  - Issue: the text calls the red-tailed hawk a top predator that nothing eats, but Figures 1A and 2 draw a hawk → owl arrow. The hawk-disease example calls the rattlesnake increase "indirect", but Figure 1A shows hawks eating rattlesnakes, which would make it direct.
  - Resolution: neither claim is tested. Direct and indirect effects use original webs with every arrow stated, and the O1 card notes that "top predator" depends on the model.
  - Sources: internal textbook inconsistency, read at 300 dpi.
- **L06-RF7** (p. 74)
  - Issue: the text says the algae themselves consumed the oxygen. Algae do respire, especially at night, but in nutrient-polluted water the largest drain is usually decomposers breaking down dead algae. The sentence is incomplete rather than wrong.
  - Resolution: Q28 is keyed to decomposition; its explanation (round 1) adds that living algae also use oxygen at night, which is the part the textbook mentions.
  - Sources: NOAA National Ocean Service, "What is a dead zone?"; USGS Water Science School, "Water Q&A: What causes fish kills?"
- **L06-RF8** (pp. 74–75)
  - Issue: the textbook says the stocked predator was pike, says fish had become hard to find, and tells the fix as two separate steps. The scientists' review (full text read) reports: sewage diversion in the mid-1970s was the main driver of recovery; over a million juvenile pikeperch were stocked in 1984–1991, before and during the 1989–1993 mass fish removal; the removal cut planktivorous roach and smelt by about 90 percent (roach were abundant, open-water predators scarce); phosphorus left the lake in harvested fish; the phytoplankton change was not driven by extra zooplankton grazing, and the mechanisms remain unclear.
  - Resolution: questions say "predatory fish". Lake items present the cascade as the model's prediction or the textbook's account (Q24, Q25 and Q27 limitations or framing). The O4 card and key idea 8 were corrected in round 1.
  - Source: Salonen et al. 2020, *Hydrobiologia* 847: 4601–4619, open-access PDF at Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) Jukuri (the repository record page returned HTTP 502 to a reviewer, so the PDF URL is cited).
- **L06-RF9** (pp. 68–69)
  - Issue: the text calls earthworms and dung beetles decomposers (often called detritivores) and says the matter would be locked away "forever."
  - Resolution: questions use only bacteria and fungi as decomposer examples, and "forever" is not used.
  - Source: National Geographic Education, "Decomposers."
- Textbook figures (bison 500 kg and up to 8 kg of grass a day; Lahti dates) are treated as the textbook's examples, not as timeless facts. Q14 says "In the textbook's example."

### Review flags and resolutions
- **L07-RF1** (pp. 77, 78, 84): Earth called closed with "none" of its matter entering or leaving.
  - The same p. 78 lists exceptions, and Earth is open to energy.
  - Resolution: content says "nearly closed for matter, open to energy". Q03 separates matter from energy, and Q04 explains why the model stays useful.
  - Sources: NASA Asteroid Fast Facts (more than 100 tons of dust per day); NASA Earth Observatory atmospheric escape (several hundred tons per day); NASA Earth Fact Sheet (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg).
  - Round 2: the textbook never says Earth is open to energy, so that half of the correction (glossary "closed system", key idea 1, O2 card, Q03) now cites NASA Earth Observatory "Climate and Earth's Energy Budget" (sunlight in is balanced by thermal infrared radiation out). The same record is on Q03, whose scope now includes p. 84.
- **L07-RF2** (pp. 79, 84): "water molecules a dinosaur drank", and the p. 84 spread says the total number of atoms *and molecules* never changes.
  - Atoms persist, but molecules are split in photosynthesis and rebuilt in respiration. Reactions change molecule counts: 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O → 1 C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ turns 12 molecules into 7.
  - Resolution: Q07 keys the atom-level revision, and the O2 card watchOut says the same. Key idea 2 and the O2 objective now say atoms are rearranged into new molecules (round 1 added the p. 84 claim and a p. 84 evidence record).
  - Sources: OpenStax Biology 2e 8.2 and 7.4.
- **L07-RF3** (pp. 79, 84): Figure 2 labels ice → vapor "Evaporation", which is really sublimation.
  - The spread says "water gas" and has a blue arrow labeled "Photosynthesis" between the cloud and soil boxes.
  - Resolution: Q09 keys sublimation, and the evaporation distractor explains the label. Q08 describes clouds as droplets. The spread is cited for its text boxes only. Round 1: the O1 card's first paragraph now teaches sublimation.
  - Sources: USGS Water Science School pages on sublimation and condensation.
- **L07-RF4** (p. 82): lightning's products "fall to Earth as ammonia".
  - Lightning makes nitrogen oxides, which reach the ground in rain as nitrates.
  - Resolution: no question says lightning makes ammonia. The O3 card and Q19's rationale say nitrates.
  - Sources: NASA Aura lightning NOx page; EarthDate "Lightning Strikes".
- **L07-RF5** (p. 82): "only one process … two ways" leaves out industrial (Haber–Bosch) fixation.
  - Resolution: Q19 keys fertilizer factories as a third way, and its rationale now names the textbook's two-way version first. The O3 card mentions factories.
  - Source: UF/IFAS EDIS SS684.
- **L07-RF6** (p. 83): "you use the nitrates in the peanut" to make your proteins.
  - Animals use amino acids from digested protein.
  - Resolution: Q24 keys amino acids and carries the nitrate claim as a distractor whose rationale now says the textbook's peanut example puts it that way. The O3 card watchOut covers it too.
  - Source: OpenStax Biology 2e 34.2.
- **L07-RF7** (p. 82): "in nearly all ecosystems … nitrates limit" growth.
  - Phosphorus often limits aquatic systems, and plants take up ammonium too.
  - Resolution: content says "often". Q20 states the soil is nitrogen-poor and tests only what one trial supports. The O3 diagram shows roots absorbing both forms.
  - Sources: OpenStax Biology 2e 46.3; UF/IFAS.
- **L07-RF8** (pp. 79–81, 85), rewritten in round 1 because the first version overstated the textbook error:
  - Figures 2–3 and p. 85 use "cellular respiration" as shorthand for the consumer → air arrow. That is acceptable, but game wording keeps cells (respiration) separate from lungs (breathing).
  - Page 80 describes a manatee exhaling underwater, with the CO₂ rising to the surface and some staying dissolved; manatees actually surface to breathe air.
  - Resolution (unchanged): Q10 says "breathes out at the surface", and no item asks where a manatee's breath CO₂ ends up. Q02 says the carbon dioxide and water come from cells.
  - Sources: USFWS Florida manatee; OpenStax 7.4.
- **L07-RF9** (p. 81): fossil fuels form "under layers of soil".
  - They actually form under sediment and rock, with heat and pressure.
  - Resolution: Q15 and the O4 card use the corrected wording.
  - Sources: EIA "Coal explained"; NASA Earth Observatory "The Carbon Cycle".
- **L07-RF10** (pp. 86–87): the Figure 5 map has no date or source, the "six places" activity can't be reproduced, and the section never says stored forest carbon can be lost again.
  - Resolution: Q27 uses an invented site table instead of the map (round 1 added an equal-size condition). The O4 watchOut covers the permanence limit and says fast growth is not the only test.
  - Round 2: Q17 was rewritten to ask what a wildfire in a reforested site means for judging carbon-capture plans (stored carbon can return to the air), Q26's storage criterion is now "keep the captured carbon out of the air for many decades", and new Q29 applies the p. 87 growing-conditions idea. The RF10 resolution text in L07.json says the same.
  - Source: NASA Earth Observatory "The Carbon Cycle".
- **L07-RF11** (p. 83): decomposers said to leave "nitrates and ammonia".
  - Decomposition releases ammonium, and nitrifying bacteria then make the nitrates.
  - Resolution: Q21 matches decomposers to ammonia.
  - Round 2 (optional science finding, applied): the O3 card's watchOut adds "(In damp soil, most ammonia is in the form scientists call ammonium.)", so the grade-7 word "ammonia" is not left unqualified.
  - Sources: UF/IFAS EDIS SS684; Minnesota Department of Agriculture "Ecological Effects of Ammonia" (at pH 6 the ammonia-to-ammonium ratio is about 1 to 3000).
- **L07-RF12** (p. 80, new in round 1): producers are said to take in carbon dioxide and use it to make oxygen gas and sugars, which implies the O₂ comes from CO₂.
  - The O₂ released in photosynthesis comes from splitting water; CO₂ supplies the carbon for sugar.
  - Resolution: Q07 and the O2 card watchOut (now explicit) say plants split water to release oxygen gas. No item says O₂ comes from CO₂, and Q10's new split-water distractor follows the same science.
  - Sources: OpenStax Biology 2e 8.2 (the record already cited in RF2).
- **L07-RF13** (p. 86, new in round 2): the page says burning fossil fuels for energy causes global climate change but gives no share, and the earlier key idea 7 said fossil fuels add "most" of the extra CO₂ with no source.
  - Resolution: key idea 7 now says burning fossil fuels is "the main source of the extra carbon dioxide that is driving climate change". No question asks about the size of the share.
  - Source: NASA Earth Observatory "The Carbon Cycle" ("the primary source of increased carbon dioxide in the atmosphere today").

  - 9 questions.
- L08-O2 (relate): original horizontality shows folding and tilting came later; faults, intrusions and erosion happen after layers form; cross-cutting relationships order them.
  - Families F04 (original horizontality and folding: Q09, Q10), F05 (cutting features: Q11 intrusion; Q12 repairs a sign that states the rule backward for eroded surfaces, faults and intrusions together, as the p. 101 callout does), F06 (features and faults: Q13, Q14), F11 (Q25, Q26).

  - 6 questions.

  - Families F02 (Q04), F09 (half-life numerics: Q20, Q21), F10 (radiometric clock, what can be dated, bracketing: Q22, Q23, Q24).

### Review flags and resolutions
- **L08-RF1** (p. 101; contradicts pp. 96–97 and p. 103)
  - Issue: the Key Science Concept callout says an eroded surface, a fault or an intrusion is *older* than any stratum it cuts. That reverses the law of cross-cutting relationships. The OCR layer misses this callout, so it was confirmed from a 250 dpi render.
  - Resolution: content teaches that the cutting feature is always younger, eroded surfaces included. Q12 asks learners to correct a trail sign that states the rule backward for eroded surfaces, faults and intrusions together (as the p. 101 callout does), and Q25 applies the rule to an eroded canyon; both carry external evidence. The O2 card warns that some printed diagrams flip the rule.
  - Sources: NPS, "Geologic Principles—Cross-cutting Relationships"; PRI Digital Atlas of Ancient Life, "Relative age dating"; textbook pp. 96, 97, 103.
- **L08-RF2** (pp. 98, 101, 103)
  - Issue: the textbook says strata with the same kinds of fossils are the same age, with no qualifier.
  - Resolution: content says *about* the same age, within the time the species lived, best narrowed by short-lived, widespread index fossils (Q17, Q18, Q19). The textbook's own p. 98 caption says "approximately the same age." The name "law of fossil succession" is kept (geologists more often say faunal succession).
  - Sources: Geosciences LibreTexts (UC Davis GEL 109), "Biostratigraphy – Biozones and Zone Fossils"; USGS, "Geologic Time: Relative Time Scale."
- **L08-RF3** (p. 103 vs p. 94)
  - Issue: the summary's "the layers on either side of the gap are the same age" is broader than Section 3, which is about *matching* layers.
  - Resolution: Q07 and Q08 talk about matching layers and add that the gap is younger.
  - Source: textbook p. 94.
- **L08-RF4** (pp. 91, 92, 102–103)
  - Issue: absolute dating is presented as igneous-only, while the vocabulary defines it for rocks, fossils and events. The lesson never explains how sedimentary layers get ages in years.
  - Resolution: content says radiometric dating works directly on igneous rock, and that sedimentary layers get age *ranges* by bracketing (Q24). Q23 explains why sand grains carry older clocks. Carbon-14 and other methods are outside this lesson and are not mentioned.
  - Sources: USGS, "Geologic Time: Radiometric Time Scale"; PRI, "Absolute age dating."
- **L08-RF5** (p. 93)
  - Issue: Grand Canyon numbers are rounded or garbled ("nearly 40 or more layers," "between 1.7 to 2 billion years"), and the record has gaps.
  - Resolution: not tested. The O1 card uses NPS figures (oldest rocks about 1.8 billion years, Kaibab rim rock about 270 million years) and mentions missing chapters.
  - Source: NPS, "Geology - Grand Canyon National Park."
- **L08-RF6** (pp. 98–99)
  - Issue: foraminifera are described in the past tense and as "animals," but they are living single-celled protists. Ammonites are called "shellfish" (they were extinct shelled cephalopods). Trilobite side facts were not checked further.
  - Resolution: no question tests group descriptions or trilobite dates. The O3 card says foraminifera still live today.
  - Sources: UCMP, "Introduction to the Foraminifera"; UCMP, "The Cephalopoda."
- **L08-RF7** (p. 97)
  - Issue: "the largest faults occur along transform boundaries" is questionable; subduction megathrusts are giant faults that produce the largest earthquakes.
  - Resolution: not used anywhere.
  - Source: USGS, "Introduction to Subduction Zones: Amazing Events in Subduction Zones."
- **L08-RF8** (pp. 91, 103)
  - Issue: the textbook gives a 4.6-billion-year Earth and says some igneous rocks are more than 4 billion years old. USGS gives 4.54 billion years. The oldest dated rocks on the USGS page, the Acasta Gneiss (about 4.03 billion years), are metamorphosed igneous rocks whose zircons record when the original igneous rock crystallized, so p. 103 is loose rather than wrong (reworded in the second review cycle). Zircon crystals and grains reach about 4.3 to 4.4 billion years (the USGS page cites both figures, re-checked 2026-10-17), and oldest-known records can change.
  - Resolution: the O4 card says roughly 4.5 billion years and credits zircon crystals. Not tested.
  - Sources: USGS, "Geologic Time: Age of the Earth"; Stern and Bleeker, "Age of the World's Oldest Rocks Refined Using Canada's SHRIMP: The Acasta Gneiss Complex," *Geoscience Canada* (abstract opened 2026-10-17: zircons from a deformed igneous rock crystallized about 4.03 billion years ago, with metamorphism later).
- **L08-RF9** (pp. 90, 100–102)
  - Issue: OCR gaps (opener photo, KSC callouts, Figure 7 labels).
  - Resolution: all pages read from renders; no content relies on OCR alone.
- **L08-RF10** (p. 102)
  - Issue: the radiometric clock model leaves out the closed-system assumption.
  - Resolution: Q20 and Q21 state a closed-system condition, Q21's limitation names potassium-40's two decay products and argon loss, and the O4 card's `watchOut` names the assumption.
  - Sources: PRI, "Absolute age dating"; USGS, "Radiometric Time Scale."
- **L08-RF11** (p. 103; added in revision round 1)
  - Issue: the Lesson Summary's superposition line drops the "undisturbed" condition that pp. 91, 93 and the p. 100 callout include, and two entries later the same summary says the oldest layer may not be on the bottom in folded rock.
  - Resolution: content always states the condition (Q01 conditions, Q03 and Q27 not-flipped conditions, Q10, the O1 card's `watchOut`). No question cites the p. 103 summary line for superposition.
  - Sources: textbook pp. 93, 95; USGS, "Geologic Time: Relative Time Scale" ("uncontorted" layers).
- **L08-RF12** (pp. 91, 95, 101, 103; added in the second review cycle)
  - Issue: the textbook states original horizontality as deposition in "horizontal" (p. 95: "flat, horizontal") layers, with no "nearly". Geologists say horizontal or nearly horizontal, so a layer can start with a gentle slope.
  - Resolution: the glossary, key ideas 1 and 4, and the O1 and O2 cards say "flat or nearly flat", and that *steeply* tilted or folded layers were moved later. Q09 (steeply tilted shale and limestone; its limitation names gentle depositional slopes) and Q27 use the same wording in their rationales.
  - Sources: textbook p. 95; NPS, "Geologic Principles—Superposition and Original Horizontality."

### Review flags and resolutions
- **L09-RF1** (p. 111)
  - Issue: the text says the Burgess Shale has yielded "over 60,000 different species". That is the scale of specimen counts, not species.
  - Resolution: no species count is used. Q15 tests why the site matters, which is that it preserves soft-bodied animals.
  - Sources: Royal Ontario Museum (about 200 species, over 150,000 specimens); UCMP "The Cambrian Period".
- **L09-RF2** (pp. 105, 112)
  - Issue: the end-Permian toll appears as 95 percent of lifeforms on p. 105 and 90 percent of species on p. 112. Outside sources also differ.
  - Resolution (updated round 1): the O3 card now says the end-Permian event was the worst and that most species died out, especially in the oceans; the earlier resolution described wording the card did not contain. No question keys a percentage, and the O3 watch-out names the disagreement.
  - Sources: NASA "The Great Dying" (about 9 in 10 marine and 7 in 10 land species); NHM London (more than 95 percent).
- **L09-RF3** (pp. 107, 116–117)
  - Issue: "only about 10 percent" for the Phanerozoic conflicts with the textbook's own numbers: 541 ÷ 4,600 ≈ 12 percent. The 541 Ma date is also out of date (538.8 Ma on ICS v2024/12).
  - Resolution: Q05 keys 12 percent (tolerance 0.5), and its limitations note both the textbook's rounding and the 538.8 Ma date. Elsewhere 541 Ma is kept as the lesson's value.
  - Sources: NPS "Geologic Time Scale" and "The Precambrian" (Precambrian about 88 percent); ICS chart.
- **L09-RF4** (p. 107)
  - Issue: "Most of the rock that makes up Earth's crust formed during the current eon" is questionable. The cores of the continents (cratons) are Precambrian. The Phanerozoic gets more chart space mainly because of its fossil record.
  - Resolution: Q06 keys the fossil-record reason, and the crust claim is not used.
  - Sources: USGS Youth and Education "Introduction"; NPS "The Precambrian"; USGS "Age of the Earth".
- **L09-RF5** (p. 110)
  - Issue: the text says cyanobacteria were "the first organisms to carry out photosynthesis" and equates stromatolites with cyanobacteria colonies. Other microbes photosynthesized earlier without releasing oxygen, stromatolites are built by microbial mats in general, and the 3.5 Ga start of oxygen release is debated.
  - Resolution: content says "first organisms known to release oxygen by photosynthesis". Q12 tests only the order of steps. Round 1: Q13 had stated the textbook's "well over a billion years" delay as fact; it now says "probably hundreds of millions of years" and its limitations record the debate. Cycle 2: Q13's limitations now say the textbook states (p. 111) a delay of more than a billion years, rather than that its timeline implies one. No question keys a start date.
  - Sources: OpenStax Biology 2e 22.1; UCMP "Cyanobacteria: Fossil Record"; round 1 added Planavsky et al. 2014 (CaltechAUTHORS record) and MIT News 2021.
- **L09-RF6** (pp. 111, 116)
  - Issue: the photo caption says all modern organisms trace back to the Cambrian Explosion. Its duration is also inconsistent (about 11 million years in the text, 541–539 Ma on the spread), and 541 Ma is out of date.
  - Resolution: content describes early relatives of most major animal groups appearing long after life began. Q14 repairs the "life began then" idea, and no question keys a duration.
  - Sources: OpenStax Biology 2e 27.4 and 22.1; ICS chart.
- **L09-RF7** (pp. 112–113)
  - Issue: the text says dinosaurs "dominated" from 230 Ma, and that the "Age of the Dinosaurs" ended at 66 Ma. In fact dinosaurs became dominant only after the end-Triassic extinction, and birds are living dinosaurs.
  - Resolution: content says "non-bird dinosaurs" for the 66 Ma extinction, and no question keys the 164-million-year figure for dominance. Round 1: Q19's table gives first dinosaurs about 230 Ma and the end of the non-bird dinosaurs at 66 Ma; its statement f uses that span only for how long they existed.
  - Sources: NHM London (Triassic page, birds page, mass-extinction page).
- **L09-RF8** (pp. 114, 118–119)
  - Issue (rewritten in cycle 2): the lesson dates the current ice age from 2.6 Ma. That fits p. 118's definition, which needs ice caps at both poles, but Antarctica alone has carried an ice cap since about 34 Ma (p. 114), so the start date depends on the definition used. The interglacial start of 11,500 years differs from the ICS Holocene base of 11,700 years. (The earlier wording said the 2.6 Ma date conflicts with the lesson's own definition; the cycle 2 science reviewer showed that p. 118 requires both poles, and NOAA uses "ice age" in both senses.)
  - Resolution (updated round 1): the O3 card now actually says that Antarctica has held an ice sheet for about 34 million years, that northern ice-sheet cycles began about 2.6 Ma and that the present interglacial began about 11,700 years ago; before round 1 no card or glossary entry said this. Following p. 118, the card also contrasts natural interglacial warming with today's far faster, mainly human-caused warming. Q22 keys no start date, and Q28 says "big ice sheets begin cycling".
  - Sources: NOAA Climate.gov; ICS chart; round 1 added NASA Science "Evidence" (climate change).
- **L09-RF9** (p. 118)
  - Issue: the Great Lakes are explained only by the weight of ice sinking the crust.
  - Resolution: Q23 and the O3 card add the ice's gouging and deepening of the land, with meltwater filling the basins afterward.
  - Source: NOAA "Great Lakes ecoregion".
- **L09-RF10** (p. 106)
  - Issue: Figure 1A labels the top of the Grand Canyon sequence as 208 Ma. NPS gives about 270 Ma for the Kaibab Formation, the rim rock.
  - Resolution: no question uses Figure 1A's ages. Q24 and Q25 use invented canyons to test the method (superposition plus lateral continuity), which the figure shows correctly.
  - Source: NPS Grand Canyon geology.
- **L09-RF11** (pp. 105, 108–109)
  - Issue: 4.6 billion years is the rounded age of the solar system. USGS gives 4.54 billion years for Earth.
  - Resolution: content dates the solar system to about 4.6 Ga. Since cycle 2 it says Earth had a core and mantle by about 4.5 Ga and its first crustal rocks by about 4.4 Ga (Figure 2 order; see RF13).
  - Source: USGS "Age of the Earth".
- **L09-RF12** (pp. 118–119)
  - Issue: the text says modern humans appeared "more than 200,000 years ago". That is true but out of date: the Smithsonian gives about 300,000 years.
  - Resolution: no question keys this date. Round 1: Q19's table lists the first modern humans at about 300,000 years ago (Smithsonian), and its statement c is false under either date.
  - Source: Smithsonian Human Origins "Homo sapiens".
- **L09-RF13** (pp. 108–109, 112–113, 117)
  - Issue: the textbook contradicts itself on two points. Figure 2 says young Earth was "entirely liquid" while the text says "almost completely molten". The text dates the start of Pangaea's breakup to about 200 Ma, while the timeline and spread give 180 Ma.
  - Resolution (updated round 1): the O2 card says "largely molten", and the O3 card now dates the breakup to "starting roughly 200 to 180 million years ago" (before round 1 no content dated it). No question keys either detail.
  - Cycle 2 addition: a third contradiction. The p. 109 text says the core, mantle and crust had formed by about 4.5 billion years ago, while Figure 2 (p. 109, rendered) puts the core at 4.5 Ga, the moon-forming impact "soon after", and the first crustal rocks at 4.4 Ga. The p. 116 spread has the same order. The O2 card had followed the text and so put the crust before the impact. It now follows Figure 2's order: core and mantle by roughly 4.5 Ga, then the impact, then the first crustal rocks by about 4.4 Ga. Q10's explanation matches. The science reviewer's reasoning: a giant impact would most likely have remelted any earlier surface, and the oldest surviving crustal minerals are about 4.4 billion years old. The card itself makes neither claim.
  - Sources: textbook pages only (pp. 108–109, 112–113, 116–117).
- **L09-RF14** (pp. 104, 107, 116–117)
  - Issue: OCR condition, as described under Source reading.
  - Resolution: all chart and spread content was read from the renders.
- **L09-RF15** (p. 115; added round 1)
  - Issue: the text says the Himalayas rise "more than one centimeter per year". That is the older USGS This Dynamic Earth figure; rates vary along the range (NASA: several millimeters a year; National Geographic: about 10 mm a year in the northwest, about 1 mm a year at Everest). Q20's explanation had repeated it as a precise fact.
  - Resolution: Q20 says the Himalayas are still rising, by up to about a centimeter a year in places. No question keys a rate.
  - Sources: USGS "The Himalayas: Two continents collide"; NASA Earth Observatory "Dhaulagiri, Himalaya"; National Geographic "Why Mount Everest keeps changing its height".
- **L09-RF16** (pp. 111, 112, 114, 115, 117; added round 1)
  - Issue: four dated or questionable details that content does not use:
    - modern whales at about 5.3 Ma, though both modern whale groups existed by the late Oligocene;
    - whales "evolved to live in the oceans" by 50 Ma, though whales then were land-living or amphibious, and fully aquatic whales appear about 40 Ma;
    - oxygen reaching today's level, with the first land plants, at 400 Ma, though land plants go back to the Ordovician and oxygen later rose as high as about 35 percent;
    - Pangaea complete only by 252 Ma, though the USGS says it had formed by the start of the Permian;
    - (e, added in cycle 2) the p. 115 timeline (14 Ma, rendered) says apes in southern European grasslands evolved into modern apes and humans, though the oldest known members of the human family lived in Africa (Sahelanthropus, Chad, about 7 to 6 Ma).
  - Resolution: none is a keyed fact. Q19's table uses NHM whale dates, and Q28 says Pangaea "exists as one supercontinent" at the end-Permian, which is true under either date. #### verify-agent, independent final verifier, round 1 (2026-10-14)
The verifier did not write or revise any of this content before this pass. What was checked for each question:
- The key is correct and the only defensible answer under the stated conditions.
- Order and classify items have exactly one defensible sequence or bin. Re-derived for Q01, Q12, Q24, Q28 and Q31 (order) and Q16, Q22 and Q27 (classify).
- Numeric answers were recomputed: Q04 2,600 ka; Q05 11.76 % → 12 %; Q30 20.66 min → 21, or 20.93 min with 4.54 Ga.

### Review flags and resolutions
- **L10-RF1** (pp. 129–130)

- **L10-RF5** (p. 134)
  - Issue: carbon dioxide and water vapor are called "elements". The percentages are dry-air values and are dated.
  - Resolution: no question tests trace-gas percentages. Q07 tests only "mostly nitrogen and oxygen" and "nearly all weather in the lowest, densest air". The "all weather" wording is handled in RF13.
  - Sources: NOAA JetStream, The Atmosphere.
- **L10-RF6** (pp. 138–139)
  - Issue:
    - Biosphere 2 was "closed" only to matter, not energy.
    - The oxygen story is simplified: concrete absorbed CO₂, and oxygen was pumped in starting about 16 months in.
    - The structure leaked a little air (under 10% a year).
    - The facility figures and "today" date from when the textbook was written.
  - Resolution:
    - Content defines a closed system as closed to matter but open to energy.
    - The O4 card says the building was built to be closed to matter and that oxygen had fallen from about 21% to about 14% by about 16 months in. It also says managers pumped in oxygen.
    - Since cycle 2, the O4 card poses the missing-CO₂ puzzle without answering it. The concrete finding appears only in Q28's feedback and in this flag.
    - Q26 asks what could cross the walls "as designed", and its conditions name the leak and the oxygen injection.

    - Q28 asks for the best hypothesis about the missing CO₂ without naming the bacteria.
    - Q29 asks what to do next with the test data.
    - Acreage and species counts are not tested.
  - Sources: EARTH Magazine; Scientific American.
- **L10-RF7** (pp. 132, 137)
  - Issue: system thickness values are rough. The biosphere is given as "more than 70 km" (National Geographic says about 20 km), and the atmosphere has no sharp top.
  - Resolution: no question tests these thicknesses. Q05 uses only the crust and mantle values, which match standard figures.
  - Sources: National Geographic, Biosphere and Mantle.
- **L10-RF8** (p. 132)
  - Issue: the textbook gives fresh water as 3% of Earth's water; USGS gives 2.5%. USGS splits fresh water into 68.7% ice caps and glaciers, 30.1% groundwater, and 1.2% surface and other fresh water.
    - That 1.2% is not just lakes and rivers. It also includes ground ice and permafrost, soil moisture, swamps, the atmosphere and living things.
    - Lakes and rivers together are only about 0.26% of all fresh water. The textbook's "1% lakes and rivers" is therefore about four times too high, though the ranking is the same.
    - Corrected in cycle 2. Round 1 had called this "slightly different rounding", which was wrong.
  - Resolution: Q06 asks only the ranking (most fresh water is in glaciers and ice caps). Q06's rationale and explanation now say lakes and rivers hold about 1 percent or less. The USGS records in RF8 and Q06 carry the lakes and rivers split.
  - Sources: USGS, Where is Earth's Water? (reopened 2026-10-17).

  - Issue: the cake-batter analogy and the conduction-only wording for outward energy flow can suggest a liquid, fast-moving mantle.
  - Resolution: content says the mantle is solid rock that creeps over many millions of years ("many" added in cycle 2). Q04 repairs the "liquid magma mantle" idea. Q25 names the scale and speed difference (loops thousands of kilometers across that take millions of years) as a real limit of the pot model. Q11 now carries a limitations note.
  - Sources: National Geographic, Mantle.

  - Issue: OCR is empty or garbled on these pages.

- **L10-RF12** (p. 137, new in reviser round 1)
  - Issue: the Key Science Concept spread says all the energy in Earth's systems comes from the sun or Earth's hot interior. Tidal energy from the Moon's gravity is a small third source, and tidal mixing may supply about half the mechanical energy that sustains the deep ocean loop.
  - Resolution:
    - Key idea 5 now says "two main power sources", and the O3 card already said "Almost all".
    - Q15 keeps the two-bin model; the sun is still defensible against the only other bin, Earth's interior. Its limitations and ocean-item rationale name winds and tidal stirring.

- **L10-RF13** (p. 134, new in reviser round 1)
  - Issue: the text says all kinds of weather happen in the lowest levels, and the caption says clouds like those pictured occur only there. NOAA says almost all weather occurs in the troposphere.

  - Sources: NOAA JetStream, Layers of the Atmosphere.
- **L10-RF14** (pp. 138–139, new in reviser round 1)
  - Issue: Section 5 states several unsupported absolutes or overclaims:
    - the other planets and moons are inhospitable to life;

- **L10-RF15** (p. 135, new in review cycle 2)
  - Issue: Section 3 says concentrated sunlight at the equator warms the air there. This can suggest that sunlight mainly heats the air directly. In fact the ground and sea absorb most of the sunlight Earth takes in (about 48% of incoming sunlight, against about 23% for the atmosphere), and they then warm the air above them. The textbook's simplification is not an error.
  - Resolution:
    - O3 card ¶2 now says most of the sunlight Earth absorbs is soaked up by the ground and sea, which then warm the air above them.
    - The O3 diagram edge from the Sun to the atmosphere now reads "uneven heating drives air convection" (it was "warms air unevenly"), and the alt text matches.
    - The new Q30's stem says the sunshine heats the ground and the ground warms the air.
  - Sources: NASA Earth Observatory, Climate and Earth's Energy Budget.
